title: Truth Resurrected: The Many Afterlives and Lessons of the Pearson Integrated Humanities Program
author: Patrick Callahan
summary: Patrick Callahan reviews a revised edition of Bob Carlson's Truth on Trial, the most exhaustive history of the University of Kansas's Pearson Integrated Humanities Program (1970-1979), which introduced freshmen to the Great Books amid the era's curricular collapse and student unrest. He traces the program's continuing influence through alumni like USCCB president Archbishop Paul Coakley and a network of boarding schools and monasteries, and argues Carlson's history rightly credits professors Dennis Quinn, Frank Nelick, and John Senior together even though popular memory now centers almost entirely on Senior. Callahan uses newly released KU archival material to make the case that Quinn's overlooked administrative skill, especially his success securing NEH funding during a university-wide payroll freeze, was as essential to the program's decade of survival as its professors' teaching. He closes arguing that the program's ultimate closure in 1977-78, driven by concern over student conversions to Catholicism, was pushed through opportunistically while Quinn was on sabbatical, and that reviving Senior's educational vision today requires also relearning Quinn's institutional praxis.
points: Callahan credits overlooked administrator Dennis Quinn, not just John Senior, as decisive to the IHP's success, citing his securing of roughly $245,500 annually in NEH funding during a university-wide payroll freeze and stagflation-era budget cuts.

The review documents the program's outsized modern legacy: alumni include USCCB president Archbishop Paul Coakley and Bishop James Conley, plus a lineage of boarding schools (St. Gregory the Great, St. Martin's, St. Andrew's) and Our Lady of Clear Creek Monastery.

Callahan argues the program's 1977-78 closure, driven by outside concern over student conversions to Catholicism, was pushed through specifically while Quinn was away on sabbatical, calling this 'the cowardice of Quinn's opponents.'
His closing thesis is that reviving Senior's educational vision for the 21st century requires also relearning Quinn's institutional praxis: 'good seeds deserve good soil.'
quotes: During its time, the professors taught hundreds of students and received national attention in 1973 when Russell Kirk spoke of it as "the most lively innovation in college programs.

Despite or because of the administrative challenges of those times, Dennis Quinn took the initiative to seek external funding from the National Endowment for the Humanities to launch the Pearson Integrated Humanities Program.

From 1971 to 1973, he brought the equivalent of $245,500 annually to KU to offset faculty, staff, and program costs. At a time when other departments were trimming speaker lists, he was bringing in Mortimer Adler and other nationally-recognized intellectuals to campus.

That these professors were known to volunteer at their local parish should never have counted against them any more than that their colleague at the time was leading instruction at a local Zen Center.

And it speaks to the cowardice of Quinn's opponents that they only pushed through the final budget cuts that would lead to the end of the program in the Spring of 1978 when Quinn was away on sabbatical.
As we move forward the educational vision of John Senior into the 21st century, we need to learn from the administrative praxis of Dennis Quinn to succeed. Good seeds deserve good soil.
